catalog_quote: [p. 8, sec. 1.6.1] Phrase-Level Stress The penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase is always lengthened. [sec. 2.1] Note that vowel length is not contrastive in Mijikenda: the penultimate vowel in a phrase is always predictably long. [p. 17, sec. 2.1.1 The Penult] The penultimate syllable of a phrase enjoys special status in Mijikenda. It is the locus of phrase-level stress (realized by vowel length alone) and it is also the most prominent position for the expression of high tones, as we shall see repeatedly. [p. 174, ch. 8] As indicated above, the penult of the phonological phrase in Mijikenda is lengthened. This, I claim, is the only effect of phrase-level stress in the language, pitch naturally being reserved for the tone system. Penultimate stress is usually explained with a trochaic foot on the final two syllables, and this is exactly what I claim for Mijikenda: every phonological phrase has a single, obligatory foot covering the final two syllables. This is how we get penultimate lengthening, and it will also allow us to derive the special status of the penult in Mijikenda tonology, as we shall soon see.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: chon1287 (Chonyi-Dzihana-Kauma, Mijikenda E72) is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Philippson 1991 (Tons et accent.., Paris V thesis, 542 pp.), was already held by the project from the DDL open copy; I read it and copied it into the chon1287 folder. It classes Mijikenda among 'langues à culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième' (§3.5.2 p.483) and gives Digo and Giryama the profile '10. accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)' (Annexe p.511), with the final syllable extrametrical and the last phrase H docking on the penult (pp.163-167, p.364 fn.1); it cites no Chonyi/Dzihana/Kauma data (Ford's 'Giryama and Chonyi notes' ms. appears only in the bibliography, p.524). The best first-hand statement for the cluster including Chonyi remains Volk 2011 (Tel Aviv PhD, already downloaded by the earlier reading, re-read here): penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase always lengthened, the only effect of phrase-level stress, a final trochaic foot; Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 (BLS 18, p.29) and Philippson 1998 §2.9 concur. No source read gives a Chonyi-specific word-stress rule; all describe penultimate demarcative lengthening at phrase level, pitch being tonal. Nothing left to acquire for this item

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mijikenda (all nine dialects, Chonyi, Jibana/Dzihana and Kauma included in the data) is a tone language (mobile H tones, depressor consonants); stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase, realized solely as vowel lengthening (vowel length otherwise non-contrastive); the penult is also the target to which pre-penultimate H tones shift/spread. A word in isolation is phrase-final, so citation forms have a lengthened (stressed) penult, e.g. Chonyi ku-kalǎːŋga, Kauma wa-káláŋgîːra.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; Volk posits a single obligatory trochaic foot over the final two syllables of each phonological phrase and no other metrical structure.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. (Tonal detail only: in Digo an H targeting the penult surfaces as rise-fall over the last two syllables; Philippson 1998 notes H reaches the final rather than penult in Digo - Digo is a different glottocode.)
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly phrase-level: penult of the phonological phrase, cued by length not pitch; Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 p.29 likewise call the Mijikenda penult 'metrically prominent' with Attraction-to-Accent applying within and across words; Philippson 1991 p.484/512 and 1998 sec. 2.9 describe Mijikenda as having a demarcative penultimate accent realized as pre-pausal lengthening ('culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur').
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted statements are made for 'Mijikenda' as a whole (nine dialects: Chonyi, Digo, Duruma, Giryama, Jibana/Dzihana, Kambe, Kauma, Rabai, Ribe), not for Chonyi alone. Volk 2011's corpus includes Chonyi (two speakers, c.3.5 h), Jibana and Kauma questionnaire recordings, and Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 cite Chichonyi, Chidzihana and Chikauma forms explicitly, so chon1287 (Chonyi-Dzihana-Kauma, ISO coh) is covered first-hand; but the same statement equally covers giry1241 Giryama, digo1243 Digo, duru1249 Duruma and the Rabai/Ribe/Kambe varieties. The two Kichonyi-specific MA theses (Mbaga 2020 UoN; Mwaboza 2022 Pwani) describe Chonyi of Kilifi South but are silent on stress.

tone.says: Autosegmental analysis of tone on Chonyi nouns and verbs in sentences (tone processes and rules, meaning-distinguishing tone); states that all Mijikenda languages show tone on some words but that tone is little studied in the group; reports Volk 2007 as identifying high, low and mid ('tonijuu, tonichini na tonikati') tones on Kigiryama nouns and verbs, with H on the final and L on the first syllable of disyllabic nouns (p. 120). Its own data are Chonyi only.
